title: Async/await: explain it, then explain how it can cause thread starvation.
description: Learn how async/await works under the hood in .NET, why it improves scalability, and the specific coding patterns that can lead to thread starvation in production.

data.text: Async/await is one of the most important productivity features in modern C#, yet it is also one of the most misunderstood. In interviews, you are often asked to explain it in plain terms first, then to identify how misuse can harm an application under load.

At its simplest, async/await is a language-level pattern that lets a method pause without blocking a thread while it waits for an operation to complete — typically I/O such as a database call, an HTTP request, or disk access. When the operation finishes, the method resumes on a captured synchronization context or thread pool thread.

When you mark a method with the `async` keyword, the C# compiler rewrites it into a state machine. Each `await` on an incomplete `Task` or `ValueTask` causes the method to return to its caller immediately, freeing the current thread to do other work.

data.title: Basic async flow
data.content: This method starts an HTTP request, releases its thread while waiting, and resumes when the response arrives.

data.text: Without `async`/`await`, you would need a callback, a manual `Task` continuation, or a blocking `.Wait()` / `.Result` call. Each of those alternatives either complicates the code or blocks a thread while waiting — which is exactly what `async`/`await` is designed to avoid.

Thread starvation occurs when the thread pool is exhausted and new work cannot start because all available threads are blocked. Even though async/await frees threads during I/O waits, certain patterns can reintroduce blocking pressure.

data.title: Common causes
items: Calling `.Result` or `.Wait()` on an async method from a synchronous context.
Using `Task.Run` inside ASP.NET Core request handlers to offload CPU work instead of doing it synchronously.
Capturing a synchronization context that forces resumed work onto a limited thread pool.
Long-running synchronous I/O hidden behind an async wrapper.

data.title: Blocking on async code
data.content: This pattern can deadlock or starve the thread pool under high load because the request thread waits synchronously instead of being released.
data.code:
// AVOID: blocking the request thread
var user = GetUserAsync(userId).Result;

data.title: Why it matters in ASP.NET Core
data.text: ASP.NET Core uses a limited thread pool by default. If every incoming request blocks a thread while waiting for I/O, the pool runs out of threads. New requests queue, latency spikes, and the app appears unresponsive even though the CPU is mostly idle.

Start with thread pool metrics. In .NET you can inspect `ThreadPool.GetAvailableThreads()` and watch the thread pool worker count in PerfView or Application Insights. If the worker count is pinned at the minimum and request latency climbs without CPU saturation, thread starvation is likely.

data.title: Remediation checklist
items: Replace `.Result` / `.Wait()` with `await` all the way up the call stack.
Avoid `Task.Run` for I/O-bound work inside ASP.NET Core request handlers.
Use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in library code that does not need the synchronization context.
Profile allocations and synchronous I/O with ETW or dotnet-trace.

data.title: Proper async flow
data.content: The request thread is released until the data is ready, keeping the thread pool healthy.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Async/await frees threads during I/O waits; blocking calls defeat this benefit.
Thread starvation appears as high latency with low CPU usage.
Always prefer `await` over `.Result` or `.Wait()` in ASP.NET Core.
Use thread pool metrics and tracing to confirm the root cause before optimizing.
data.takeaway: Async/await improves throughput only when the entire call chain is truly asynchronous.
